name: Yalarnnga
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Breen, Gavan & Barry J. Blake. 2007. The grammar of Yalarnnga: a language of western Queensland. Pacific Linguistics 584. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, RSPAS, ANU. xi+120 pp. ISBN 978-0-85883-567-2. Open access:https://openresearch-repository.anu.edu.au/handle/1885/146740
catalog_quote: Primary stress, heard as greater loudness, fell regularly on the first vowel of a word and a secondary stress was irregularly heard on the third syllable of a four-syllable word or the first syllable of a disyllabic bound morpheme. Further secondary stresses may be heard later in a long word, two or more syllables after the previous stress and not on the final syllable. Some examples, with morpheme boundaries shown by hyphens and stresses by acute (primary) and grave (secondary) accents, are: yírri ‘man’, mángurru ‘dog’, pírlapirla ‘child’, ngálangà-ma ‘speaks’, yálarnnga-ya ‘in Yalarnnga’, wámarrì-yu ‘snake (ergative)’, pínka-yàma-ma ‘scratching oneself’, wántha-ma-nhàti ‘(rain) falling this way’, yúnkunhì-mu-nhàti ‘came back’.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (632 KB born-digital PDF, text, 132 PDF pages; the PDF's metadata: Acrobat Distiller 2007, title page 'The grammar of Yalarnnga.. Pacific Linguistics 584', ISBN 9780858835672) with extracted text. Page mapping confirmed: p.22 = printed p.10, p.23 = printed p.11, p.24 = printed p.12, so the locator '§2.3 Stress, pp. 11-12 (PDF pages 23-24)' is exact. The quoted passage is present verbatim at the head of §2.3 (printed p.11, p.23): 'Primary stress, heard as greater loudness, fell regularly on the first vowel of a word and a secondary stress was irregularly heard on the third syllable of a four-syllable word or the first syllable of a disyllabic bound morpheme. Further secondary stresses…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of every word. Secondary stress is irregular: typically on the third syllable of a four-syllable word or on the first syllable of a disyllabic bound suffix, with further secondaries at least two syllables after the previous stress and never on the final syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Irregularly heard on the third syllable of a four-syllable word or the first syllable of a disyllabic bound morpheme; further secondaries in long words two or more syllables after the previous stress, never word-final (examples: pínka-yàma-ma, wántha-ma-nhàti, yúnkunhì-mu-nhàti). Morphology-sensitive rather than purely rhythmic.
new_statements.exceptions: 'A number of seemingly random exceptions' attributed to speaker age and lack of practice; one probably genuine exception is reduced stress on pronouns (nhína-ma ngìya 'I'm sitting'), alternatively transfer of that reduced stress to the final syllable of the preceding word (wárrka-niyi-kà nhawa 'you might fall'); also movement of main stress off an initial /yi/ syllable to the next (yimata-ta 'for fish'; yiyarlima heard with stress shift and /yi/+/y/ coalescence).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word including suffixes); data are from recordings of the last speakers in the late 1960s-1970s, so the description is impressionistic (stress 'heard as greater loudness') and the authors flag speaker uncertainty.
new_statements.identity_note: Breen & Blake 2007 describe Yalarnnga proper (glottocode yala1262, ISO ylr; older spelling Jalanga/Yallunga/Yelina), based on recordings of the last three speakers (Mick and Lardie Moonlight, Maudie Hayden) from 1967-1979; no dialect division is recognised ('No alternative names are known for the language', p. 2). The scan's prior classification the named source could not be reached is now resolved: the grammar is open access at the ANU repository (handle 1885/146740).

sources.note: §2.3 'Stress' (pp. 11-12): primary stress (greater loudness) regularly on the first vowel of the word; secondary stress irregularly on the 3rd syllable of a 4-syllable word or the first syllable of a disyllabic bound morpheme, further secondaries two or more syllables after the previous stress and never on the final syllable; sporadic exceptions (reduced stress on pronouns, stress shift off an initial /yi/ syllable).
Phonology tables note allophones 'in unstressed or lax positions' and 'when stressed'; no statement of stress placement; cites Breen & Blake 2007 as its source.
